source.title: Open Problems on Avoidable Patterns in Partial Words

accepted.question_text: For finite patterns, where a pattern is a word over variables such as alpha, beta, and gamma, and avoidability means that there exists an infinite word avoiding that pattern, what is the computational complexity of deciding whether a given pattern p is avoidable?
Given a finite pattern p and an integer k, is it decidable whether p is k-avoidable, meaning whether there exists an infinite word over a k-letter alphabet that avoids p?

In partial-word pattern avoidance, determine the avoidability index of the binary pattern alpha beta beta alpha. A partial word may contain holes, and the avoidability index of a pattern is the smallest alphabet size k for which an infinite partial word over k letters avoids the pattern, with infinity used when no such alphabet size exists.

For ternary patterns in partial-word avoidability, where ternary patterns are patterns over the three variables alpha, beta, and gamma, determine the avoidability indices of such patterns, or at least bounds for those indices; also determine a bound on the length of unavoidable ternary patterns.

For every binary pattern p and alphabet size k, classify p with respect to minimum hole sparsity and non-trivial minimum hole sparsity in partial words. Here a partial word is lambda-sparse when every factor of length lambda contains at least one hole; minimum hole sparsity is the smallest positive lambda for which there exists an infinite lambda-sparse partial word over k letters that avoids all occurrences of p, while the non-trivial version only requires avoiding non-trivial occurrences. Determine this lambda for each p and k, or determine that it is infinite when no such partial word exists.

For abelian powers in partial words, determine the minimum alphabet size needed to construct a partial word with infinitely many holes that avoids abelian third powers, fourth powers, and fifth powers. In this setting, abelian n-freeness means that the holes can be filled with alphabet letters so that the word contains no n consecutive factors that are permutations of one another.

How densely can infinitely many holes be inserted into an abelian n-free word so that the resulting partial word remains abelian n-free? Constantly bounded spacing between consecutive holes is ruled out by the cited result, so the question asks whether the gaps can be made smaller than exponential spacing, for example with distances between consecutive holes bounded by a polynomial.

For binary patterns p in abelian pattern avoidance for partial words, improve the known sufficient length bound: the source states that if the length of p is at least 360, then there exists a binary partial word with infinitely many holes that avoids p in the abelian sense. What smaller bound, if any, can replace 360 while preserving that conclusion?
